opus-5.5.text:
I think the definition is going to keep moving, and honestly that's probably a healthy thing. If you had shown people five or ten years ago what today's models can do, writing code, reasoning through hard problems, holding a real conversation, a lot of them would have said, "Well, that's AGI." But now that we have it, people say, "No, that's just a really good chatbot," and the goalposts shift.

So my guess is there won't be a single moment where everyone agrees we crossed the line. It'll be more gradual. Each year more people will say "yeah, by my definition we're there," while others push the bar higher, maybe to systems that can do novel science on their own, or run a big chunk of a company, or meaningfully speed up the rate of discovery.

Personally, I've started caring less about the term itself and more about the impact. Is this making people dramatically more capable? Is it discovering new knowledge? Is it changing how the economy works? Those questions are more useful than arguing over a label. And I suspect when we look back, people will say we passed AGI somewhere along the way and the world kept going. It changed a lot, but it didn't feel like one dramatic switch flipping.

r001.rationale: The candidate predicts that each year more people will say AI has reached AGI by their definition.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that it's going to keep moving, and that's mostly a good thing. Every time a system does something that would have counted as AGI five years earlier, people look at it for a few weeks, get used to it, and then say, "well, sure, but it can't do X." And then it does X, and the goalposts move again. That's happened with chess, with Go, with writing, with code, with solving math problems that were supposed to be out of reach.

So I've become fairly skeptical that there's going to be a single moment where everyone agrees, "okay, that's it, we've crossed the line." I used to think it would be more of a discrete event. Now I think it's going to feel much more like the way people think about the internet. There was no day when the internet "arrived." It just gradually became woven into everything, and at some point you look back and realize the world is completely different.

What I expect is that the word "AGI" itself gets less useful over time. People will argue about definitions, and the argument will matter less and less, because the practical question becomes: what can these systems actually do, and how much of the economy and of science and of daily life is being transformed. I think in a few years people will be much more interested in things like, can it make a genuine scientific discovery, can it run a company, can it do a week of work on its own without someone checking in. Those are concrete, and they're more useful than a fuzzy label.

The other thing I'd say is that judgments are going to be very uneven across people. Someone who uses these tools all day for their job will have a totally different sense of where we are than someone who tried a chatbot once in 2023 and thought it was a cute toy. That gap is already huge, and I think it gets wider before it closes.

And then, at some point, I think the whole thing flips. Instead of asking "is this AGI yet," people will be asking "wait, when did that happen?" They'll look at what their kids take for granted, or what a small team can build, and they'll realize they missed the moment because there wasn't one. It'll have been gradual, and then it'll feel sudden in retrospect.

r001.rationale: The response predicts shifting definitions and a gradual, retrospective realization that AGI has arrived, but it does not say that the number of people who believe AI has reached AGI will increase from year to year.

astra-6.text:
I think the goalposts will keep moving. Something that would have seemed like clear evidence of AGI five years ago can happen today, and people say, “Well, sure, but it can’t do this other thing.” We get used to new capabilities remarkably quickly.

So I expect it to be less of a single moment where everybody agrees and more of a gradual change in how people think about these systems. Some people will say we’re there; others will point to something important that’s still missing. Eventually, the argument about the label may matter much less than what the systems can actually do and how that changes people’s lives.

r001.rationale: The response predicts changing views and growing disagreement about the AGI label, but does not say that the number of people who believe AI has reached AGI will increase from year to year.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’ll be much more gradual and messier than people expect. Before we have a system that most people would call AGI, some people will say we’re already there, and other people will say we’re nowhere close. And even after we have something that seems to satisfy the definitions people use today, I suspect there will still be a lot of disagreement.

Part of that is that we adapt incredibly quickly. Something feels astonishing the first time you see it, and a few months later it’s just a tool you expect to work. So I think people’s judgments will depend less on a single milestone and more on whether these systems are actually changing their lives—what they can help people do, what work they can take on, and how reliably they can do it.

r001.rationale: The response predicts ongoing disagreement and changing judgments, but it does not say that the number of people who believe AI has reached AGI will increase year to year.
